presenceLabel: Delaware (Lenape) town, raid or claim in this area
presenceNote: Delaware (Lenape) towns were in Ohio from the 1740s–50s (the Moravian towns on the Tuscarawas date from 1772; Gnadenhutten, 8 Mar 1782); Kentucky use was seasonal hunting (Henderson 1992) and war parties (1780, 1782). The Delaware valley in Pennsylvania is shown from a 1600 display start; its three counties are an inference from the Walking Purchase and the river valley, at low confidence. The winter-camps story is shown as c.1750–1775: the start is vague and the end follows Henderson’s “by the 1770s” (low confidence). The 1804 cession is shown as ten Indiana counties, an approximate area.
overlapNote: Shawnee, Mingo, Miami and Wyandot used the same hunting country (Henderson). The 1785 Fort McIntosh land was shared with the Wyandot. The White River claim was derived from the Miami (who disputed it) and the Piankashaw (who disputed the 1804 cession); Art. 5 of the 1804 treaty made the cession void if the Piankashaw would not agree, which the Piankashaw treaty of 27 Aug 1804 then did.
basis: Treaty texts (Fort McIntosh 1785, Greenville 1795, Delaware 1804, Grouseland 1805), Delaware Nation history page, State Dept diplomacy page on Fort Pitt, Wikipedia for Bird 1780 and Bryan Station. Counties for the 1804 cession are an approximation of the treaty line.

eras.label: Before c.1750 · Delaware valley, Pennsylvania (inference)
eras.text: The Delaware Nation’s homelands lay in eastern Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware, with parts of New York, Connecticut and Maryland. The Walking Purchase of 1737 took land between the forks of the Delaware and Lehigh rivers, and Lenape bands were pushed west into Ohio (Delaware Nation). The tint (Philadelphia, Bucks and Northampton counties, Pennsylvania) is an inference from the Delaware River valley and the Walking Purchase, not a sourced boundary, and New Jersey is not drawn. 1600 is a display start, not a dated beginning.
eras.apprTag: Approximate general area · inferred from the Delaware valley, low confidence
eras.mapSubLabel: approximate general area · before c.1750 · inferred

eras.label: c.1750–1771 · Winter and hunting camps
eras.text: Forced out of eastern Pennsylvania after the 1737 Walking Purchase, Lenape bands moved into Ohio (Delaware Nation). The tint is an approximate general area of their Ohio towns (Muskingum and Tuscarawas valleys), built from whole counties. Henderson (1992): small Shawnee, Mingo, Delaware, Miami and Wyandot hunting camps lay south of the Ohio in the mid-1700s, were moved north after Fort Stanwix, and hunting parties became raiding parties in the 1770s. No Delaware camp site in Kentucky is documented, so none is drawn.
eras.apprTag: Approximate general area · towns north of the Ohio

eras.label: 1772–1777 · Moravian Lenape towns on the Tuscarawas
eras.text: In 1772 the Moravian mission towns of Schoenbrunn and Gnadenhutten were founded on the Tuscarawas River in Tuscarawas County, Ohio (National Park Service). The tint is an approximate general area of the Ohio towns (Muskingum and Tuscarawas valleys), built from whole counties; only Gnadenhutten is drawn as an approximate point. No Delaware camp site in Kentucky is documented, so none is drawn.

eras.label: 1778–1782 · Fort Pitt, Gnadenhutten, Bryan Station
eras.text: 17 Sept 1778: White Eyes, Killbuck and Captain Pipe signed the Treaty of Fort Pitt. White Eyes died about two months later; Brodhead burned Lenape towns 1779-81; on 8 Mar 1782 militia killed 96 Christian Lenape at Gnadenhutten. Many Lenape then fought with the British and were at the Aug 1782 Bryan Station siege. The tint is the approximate general area of their Ohio towns, where those war parties set out from. The Moravian Lenape were moved to Sandusky in 1781 (National Park Service).

eras.label: 1780 · Bird’s invasion
eras.text: In June 1780 Bird's British and Native force (Shawnee, Odawa, Ojibwe, Delaware, Wyandot and others) came down the Great Miami, went up the Licking and took Ruddle's and Martin's Stations; captives were divided among the nations and many stayed with them until exchanges after Greenville (1795). The Delaware in the force came from their Ohio towns (tinted general area, approximate). Only the Licking reach inside Kentucky is drawn.
eras.apprTag: Approximate general area · route solid in Kentucky

eras.label: 1785–1795 · Fort McIntosh and Greenville
eras.text: Fort McIntosh (21 Jan 1785) allotted about a third of Ohio to the Wyandot and Delaware; Greenville (3 Aug 1795) ceded the east and south. The hatched counties are a rough county approximation of the allotment, north of the legs of the line the treaty text lets us place; the tint is the general area of the Delaware towns. Neither is a boundary. The Moravian Lenape later built Pilgerruh on the Cuyahoga (1786–87) and New Salem on the Huron River (1787), and went on to Ontario in 1791–92 (National Park Service); those sites are not drawn.
eras.apprTag: Approximate area · county approximation of the allotment

eras.label: 1804–1805 · White River claim and cession
eras.text: Art. 4 of the 18 Aug 1804 treaty: the United States would treat the Delawares as owners of the country between the White River (north), the Ohio (south), the Greenville line (east) and the Fort Wayne and Vincennes tracts (west). The Miami said they had only allowed the Delawares to occupy it; the Delawares gave the claim up on 21 Aug 1805 at Grouseland. The southern Indiana cession they made in 1804 is shown as ten counties, an approximate area (the Piankashaw said they gave the land to the Delawares “about thirty-seven years ago”, c.1768). The White River claim itself is text only: White River is not on the base map.

properties.kind: county list (cession, general area, outside Kentucky)
properties.note: General area only. Treaty text (Delaware 18 Aug 1804 Art. 1; Piankeshaw 27 Aug 1804 Art. 1): the tract between the Ohio and Wabash rivers, below Clark's Grant, the Vincennes tract and the Vincennes-to-Falls road, the north edge a line parallel to that road and within half a mile of its northernmost bend. Royce's map key (NPS) labels it No. 7, 'in the southern part of the State'. I approximated it by the ten Indiana counties that lie wholly or almost wholly south of a straight Vincennes-Clarksville chord (Crawford, Dubois, Gibson, Harrison, Perry, Pike, Posey, Spencer, Vanderburgh, Warrick; computed from Census county polygons). The real north edge follows the Vincennes road (Buffalo Trace), not county lines, and Clark's Grant (Clark, Floyd, Scott area) is excluded. Edges are county-ragged and low-confidence; a surveyed Royce sheet would replace this.
Main-map extent: general areas (whole-county shapes, approximate), solid lines in Kentucky and sourced points.
